'''''Physocarpus capitatus''''', commonly called '''Pacific ninebark''' or '''tall ninebark''', is a species of ''[[Physocarpus]]'' in the [[Rosaceae|rose family]] native to western [[North America]].

== Description ==
''Physocarpus capitatus'' is a dense deciduous [[shrub]] growing to {{convert|1-2.5|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall. The reddish-gray [[Bark (botany)|bark]], which is flaky and peels away in many irregular thin layers.

The [[leaves]] are distinctively grape or [[maple]]-like, palmately lobed, and {{convert|3|-|14|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} long and broad. They are deeply veined with double-toothed margins, and are a dark, shiny green on top.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Verlinde |first=Sarah |title=Pacific ninebark - The North Creek Wetland |url=https://www.uwb.edu/wetlands/plants/physocarpus-capitatus |access-date=2021-05-06 |website=[[University of Washington Bothell]]}}</ref>

It has clusters of small, creamy white [[flower]]s with five petals and numerous red-tipped stamens, which appear in late spring and persist into midsummer.

The unique [[fruit]] is an inflated glossy red pod about {{Convert|6|mm|in|frac=4}} long which turns dry and brown and then splits open to release [[seed]]s.

== Etymology ==
The common name 'ninebark' comes from the appearance of the flaky bark, seeming to have many layers.<ref name=":1" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is found at low and middle elevations in southern [[Alaska]] east to [[Montana]] and [[Utah]], and south to southern [[California]]. It is most common west of the [[Cascade Range|Cascades]] and [[Sierra Nevada]], often abundant on the north slopes of coastal mountains. It is less prevalent in the east of its range, where it overlaps with that of the [[Physocarpus malvaceus|mallow ninebark]].

It is often found in [[wetland]]s, but also forms thickets along rivers and in moist forest habitats. While it grows most robustly in wet environments, it is [[drought-tolerant]] to a degree. It prefers partial shade, but tolerates full sun and is adapted to many different soil types.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last1=Gonzalves |first1=Pete |last2=Darris |first2=Dale |date=June 28, 2007 |title=Plant Fact Sheet- PACIFIC NINEBARK Physocarpus capitatus |url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/orpmcfs7180.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150914195752/http://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/orpmcfs7180.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 14, 2015 |access-date=2021-05-06 |website=[[Natural Resources Conservation Service]] |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
Although it has low palatability for [[Browsing (herbivory)|browsing]] [[ungulate]]s, Pacific ninebark provides good cover and nesting sites for birds and small mammals.<ref name=":1" /> The seeds are eaten by birds, and persist in the seed heads until winter.<ref name=":0" />

== Toxicity ==
Some consider the plant toxic.<ref name=":1" />

== Uses ==
Pacific ninebark was used as an emetic and a laxative by [[Native Americans in the United States|indigenous groups]].<ref name=":1" /> The stems were used to make children's hunting bows and small items such as needles; straighter shoots were used to make arrows. The bark was mixed with cedar bark to make a dark brown dye.<ref name=":0" />

It is used in [[ecological restoration]] due to its fibrous roots which are good for [[Erosion control|bank stabilization]], and its ability to grow from cuttings.<ref name=":1" /> Furthermore, it does not need an overhead canopy to become established at a restoration site as it is tolerant of direct sun. It may grow aggressively enough to shade out [[invasive species]] such as [[reed canary grass]] and [[Himalayan blackberry]].<ref name=":0" /> It is popular in California as a garden plant.
